title: The Metric War
logline: Two teams report two numbers for completed trips, and Marcus rebuilds the model, the lake, the Spark jobs and the warehouse until the board sees one number everyone trusts.

modules.logline: Marcus finds that the trip number war starts with a model nobody declared, and learns to state the grain before anything else.
scenes: Monday's board pack shows 412,000 completed trips on Kofi's dashboard and 398,500 in Finance's report. Asha asks which is right. Marcus opens both queries and finds no shared table, no shared row. What should one row actually mean?

At the design review Kofi sketches one giant trips table with everything in it. Finance wants every lookup split into its own table. Marcus walks them through Kimball's four steps. Should the city sit in a star or a snowflake?

Lena finds that rider_id 10442 belongs to two different people after last year's app migration. Kofi's joins merge them silently. Marcus asks her a question she is nervous to answer: which key should the warehouse own?

A rider upgrades to Plus on the 14th. Kofi's dashboard counts all her March trips as Plus revenue; Finance counts half. Both feel right. Which attribute changes deserve history, and which can simply be overwritten?

Lena backfills the rider tier dimension from two years of daily snapshots. Some riders now have overlapping versions, and one has fourteen. Marcus asks her where each version really starts. How do daily snapshots become clean SCD2 rows?

Kofi wants ninety days of rider activity without scanning ninety days of trips. Then the fraud team asks which drivers share phones. Over Friday coffee Grace says, "Pick the shape the question needs." Which shape fits each question?
teasers: Kofi brings a whiteboard sketch of one giant table, and Finance hates it.
A single rider_id turns out to belong to two different people.
A Plus upgrade in the middle of March splits revenue between two teams.
Lena backfills two years of history, and one rider ends up with fourteen versions.
Kofi wants ninety days of activity without paying for ninety days of scans.
Next week: both teams count trips, but they are counting different events.
modules.boss: Weekend review: last quarter's Plus revenue changed overnight because Kofi's dashboard joins every trip to the rider's current tier. Marcus must explain the grain, the keys and the SCD type that would have stopped it.
modules.finale: The trip dimensions are agreed, with surrogate keys and SCD2 on rider tier. Kofi shakes on it, then adds, "The real fight is the facts." He is right: the two counts still differ by 13,500.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks, "What did you build today?" Marcus says, "A rule for what one line in our big list means, so everyone counts the same thing."

modules.logline: Marcus traces the gap in trip counts to the facts themselves: which event counts, how duplicates slip in, and why money is never edited in place.
scenes: Kofi counts a trip when the app fires trip_completed. Finance counts it when the payment settles. Same trip, two events, sometimes on different days. Marcus writes the five W's on the whiteboard. Which event is the fact?

Tom wants to know how long trips take from request to payment. A transaction fact cannot answer it cheaply, and Dev suggests a daily snapshot. Marcus lists the four fact types. Which one tracks a lifecycle?

Saturday's trip_completed count is 6% higher than the number of trips drivers were paid for. Lena spots the cause first: the app retries on weak networks. How do you keep exactly one row per trip, every time?

Finance edits fares in place when a refund lands, so last month's totals quietly change. Lena notices the unexplained 2% revenue gap is largest in months with many refunds. How should a correction be recorded?

Kofi wants city name and rider tier copied onto every trip row so his dashboard stops joining. Finance worries the copies will drift. Marcus has to decide how wide the trip fact should be, and what that costs.

The ninety-day retention query reads and shuffles ninety rows per rider and takes twenty minutes. Grace says, "Store the shape of the question, not of the event." Could one row per rider per month answer it?
teasers: Tom asks a lifecycle question that a plain transaction fact cannot answer.
Saturday's trip count is 6% higher than the trips drivers were paid for.
A refund rewrites last month's revenue, and Lena notices a pattern in the 2% gap.
Kofi asks for city and tier on every trip row. Finance says no.
A twenty-minute retention query meets an idea: a whole month in one row.
Next week: Kofi wants his wide table everywhere, and Asha asks what each layer is for.
modules.boss: Weekend review: a retry storm doubled trip_completed events on Saturday, and Kofi's dashboard celebrated a record day. Marcus must show the grain, the deduplication rule and the idempotent load that would have kept the count honest.
modules.finale: Both teams sign off on one trip fact: one row per completed trip, deduplicated, with refunds as reversing ledger entries. Lena's 2% gap stays open. Asha asks the next question: which model belongs at each stage?
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why a shop receipt has a minus line. Marcus says, "When we get money wrong, we never rub it out; we write a new line that fixes it."

modules.logline: Marcus maps a model to every layer of the platform, from raw events to features, and stops broken tables before they reach the board.
scenes: Kofi proposes his wide table for everything: raw events, Finance reports and the cancellation model. It works well for his dashboard. Marcus is not sure it works for anyone else. Can one data model serve every stage?

Marcus drafts a table with one row per stage: raw, cleaned, business, serving. Dev asks what goes wrong if the raw layer is a star schema. Each stage needs a model and an anti-pattern to avoid. Which goes where?

The payments team adds a column overnight and renames another, and three payment sources must merge into one cleaned layer. Lena asks whether Data Vault is worth the extra tables. When do hubs, links and satellites pay off?

A trip with two promos appears twice in Kofi's promo dashboard, inflating discount spend by 9%. His wide table cannot split it. Marcus sketches a bridge table. How should one trip be shared between two promos?

The cancellation model scores brilliantly offline and fails in production. Lena finds that training joined today's rider statistics onto old trips. Marcus asks her one question: what did the model actually know at request time?

A half-written trips table reaches the board dashboard for twenty minutes before the job finishes, and Kofi takes the questions. Grace says, "Nobody should ever see your work in progress." How do you publish only what passed?
teasers: Marcus drafts one table that gives every platform stage its own model.
Payments renames a column overnight, and three sources must become one.
Two promos on one trip inflate Kofi's discount numbers by 9%.
The cancellation model is brilliant offline and useless in production. Why?
A half-written table reaches the board dashboard, and Kofi takes the heat.
Next week: Asha wants one trip to travel the whole platform, end to end, by Friday.
modules.boss: Weekend review: the board saw half a trips table for twenty minutes. Marcus walks through the stage map, the model chosen for each layer and the write-audit-publish gate that would have kept broken data hidden.
modules.finale: Marcus walks Asha through every stage in forty-five minutes using a seven-step method. Kofi, quietly, backs the plan. Asha approves the map, then says, "Now show me one trip moving through all of it, by Friday."
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why school has a coat room and a lunch room. Marcus says, "Different rooms for different jobs, and our data needs different shapes for different jobs too."

modules.logline: Marcus builds the thinnest pipeline that runs end to end, from a ride event to a SQL answer, and learns why every step must survive a rerun.
scenes: Asha wants one ride event to travel from the app to a SQL answer by Friday. Marcus itches to perfect the Kafka layer first, and Dev bets he will not finish. Why build every layer badly before any layer well?

The old Hadoop cluster still holds three years of trips, and its NameNode has no standby. Dev refuses to touch it. Marcus must choose where new events land. What breaks if the NameNode dies, and what does object storage change?

Lena's Kafka consumer crashes, restarts, and forty trips are missing. She committed offsets before writing them. Marcus draws partitions and consumer groups on a napkin. Where should a consumer start after a crash?
Lena's first Spark job collects a day of trips to the driver to count them, and the driver runs out of memory. She almost hides it, then asks. Who should do the counting: the driver or the executors?
Dev shows Marcus forty Airflow DAGs with no owners, and one that has failed silently since March. Marcus writes the skeleton's first DAG with data intervals. What does a run for 09:00 actually cover?
Kofi asks how many trips Meridian did yesterday, and Marcus asks five questions back before writing any SQL. Then Lena reruns the 09:00 hour by hand after a fix. What happens when a job runs twice?
teasers: Dev refuses to touch a Hadoop cluster whose NameNode has no backup.
Lena's Kafka consumer crashes, restarts, and forty trips simply disappear.
Lena's first Spark job brings down the driver, and she almost hides it.
Dev opens forty Airflow DAGs with no owners, and one has failed since March.
Kofi asks a simple question, and Lena reruns an hour by hand.
Next week: Finance wants eighteen months of trips queryable in under ten seconds.
modules.boss: Weekend review: Bengaluru shows twice as many completed trips for the 09:00 hour as the app does, because a rerun appended instead of overwriting. Marcus must make every hop idempotent and explain it to Kofi.
modules.finale: One ride event travels from generator to Kafka, Spark, object storage and SQL, scheduled by Airflow, and a small LLM script explains failed runs to Dev. It is thin, but it walks. Then Finance tries an eighteen-month query.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why Marcus built something badly on purpose. He says, "I built a tiny version of every part first, so I know they all fit together."

modules.logline: Marcus moves raw trips from loose Parquet into an Iceberg table, and learns that every fast query is one that reads fewer bytes.
scenes: Finance's eighteen-month trips query takes four minutes, and Finance wants ten seconds. Dev suggests a bigger cluster. Marcus opens the query profile instead and sees most of the time spent reading. How do you read fewer bytes?

Raw trip events still land as JSON, eighty columns wide, and Finance reads five of them. Lena asks whether Parquet, Avro or ORC is best. Marcus says it depends on who writes and who reads. Which fits analytics?

Lena partitions the trips table by rider_id and creates four million directories. Listing them alone takes minutes. Marcus asks what Finance actually filters on. Which column makes a good partition, and when is bucketing better?

Yesterday's trips return zero rows on Kofi's dashboard. The files exist, but the Hive Metastore never registered the new partition. Kofi, for once, asks Marcus for help. Why does a Hive table trust directories nobody validates?

Marcus proposes Iceberg. Dev, sceptical of new tools, asks what it solves that Hive does not. Marcus draws snapshots, manifests and column ids on the whiteboard. Can a table really be a tree of metadata?

After a week of hourly writes, the Finance query has gone from two seconds to forty. The table now holds ten thousand tiny files. Grace says, "Every table needs a janitor." What should compaction run, and how often?
teasers: Lena asks which file format wins, and Marcus answers with a question.
One partitioning choice creates four million directories overnight.
Yesterday's trips vanish from Kofi's dashboard, though every file is still there.
Marcus proposes Iceberg, and Dev wants to know what it actually fixes.
A two-second Finance query now takes forty, and nobody changed the SQL.
Next week: festival season starts, and Bengaluru brings 80% of the trips.
modules.boss: Weekend review: the Finance query slowed twentyfold under ten thousand tiny files, and a renamed fare column turned a week of fares into NULLs. Marcus must explain compaction, Iceberg column ids and the DAG that keeps the table healthy.
modules.finale: Eighteen months of trips answer in under ten seconds, and Dev's maintenance DAG compacts the table every night. Failure alerts now arrive as structured fields, not prose. Then the nightly enrichment job warns: festival week starts Monday.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why Marcus tidied files all day. He says, "Finding one big book on a shelf is quicker than finding a thousand loose pages."

modules.logline: Festival week puts 80% of trips in Bengaluru, and Marcus learns to read a Spark job, find the skew and fix it without buying more machines.
scenes: Festival week starts, and the nightly enrichment job joining thirty days of trips to drivers and zones runs past breakfast. Tom asks why the morning dashboard is empty. Marcus opens the Spark UI. Where does the time go?

Marcus reads the physical plan and sees the trip date filter applied after the join, not at the scan. Lena wrapped it in a Python UDF last month. What does Catalyst need before it can push a filter down?
The join stage writes 400 GB of shuffle for a 120 GB input. Dev asks why joining two tables moves so much data across the network. Marcus has to explain, step by step, what a shuffle really does.

The zones table has two hundred rows, yet Spark shuffles it alongside thirty days of trips. Drivers holds half a million rows. Lena suggests broadcasting both. Which join strategy fits each table, and why not both?

On the stage page, the median task finishes in eight seconds and one task runs for fifty minutes. It holds every Bengaluru trip, and Kofi's festival report waits on it. How do you split a key with 80% of the rows?

Adaptive query execution splits the skewed partition, but executors now spill to disk and one dies out of memory. Mei asks why the Spark bill doubled. Grace says, "Fix the data before you buy machines." How big should an executor be?
teasers: Marcus reads the plan and finds the date filter in the wrong place.
A 120 GB job writes 400 GB of shuffle, and Dev wants to know why.
A two-hundred-row table is being shuffled with thirty days of trips.
One task runs for fifty minutes. It holds every Bengaluru trip.
The skew is fixed, an executor dies anyway, and Mei arrives with the bill.
Next week: Finance's total for last Tuesday keeps changing, and nobody touched it.
modules.boss: Weekend review: on festival night the enrichment job went from twenty minutes to three hours, then failed at 40%. Bengaluru held 80% of the rows. Marcus must present three fixes, in order, with the evidence for each.
modules.finale: The job is back to twenty minutes in festival week, and Marcus's agent now reads plans and event logs to explain slow stages. Mei approves the smaller cluster. Then Finance's number for last Tuesday changes again.
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why one checkout queue was so long. Marcus says, "Everyone from the biggest city stood in one line, so we opened more tills just for them."

modules.logline: Marcus and Kofi build a dbt warehouse on Snowflake that gives Operations and Finance the same answer, survives late data and earns the board's trust.
scenes: Operations says 412,000 trips yesterday. Finance says 398,500. Asha puts Marcus and Kofi in one room, and both show correct SQL. Kofi admits the word itself is the problem. What does completed actually mean at Meridian?

Lena finds 2,300 trips missing from the new star schema. Their driver_id is NULL, and the inner join drops them. Kofi asks whether the fact should just allow NULL keys. What should a dimension offer for unknown?

A driver moves from Pune to Bengaluru. Overnight, all his Pune trips from last year move to Bengaluru on the dashboard, and the city leads notice. Which slowly changing dimension type keeps history where it happened?

Kofi writes his first dbt model and asks Marcus to review it. They agree on staging, intermediate and marts folders, and Lena adds the tests. What should a dbt test catch before the board ever sees a number?

Finance's total for last Tuesday keeps changing. Trips completed at 23:58 arrive two days late, and the incremental filter never sees them. Lena proposes a lookback window. How many days, and what does it cost?

Tom wants analysts to ask questions in plain English. The text-to-SQL bot answers confidently and wrongly, because completed still has two meanings. Grace says, "Teach the definitions before the machine." What must the agent see, and with which role?
teasers: Two thousand trips disappear from the star schema, and a NULL is to blame.
A driver moves city, and a year of his trips moves with him.
Kofi writes his first dbt model and asks Marcus to review it.
Finance's Tuesday total changes again. Some trips arrive two days late.
Tom wants analysts to ask the warehouse questions in plain English.
Next season: Tom wants everything real time, and the SQL bot meets the CEO.
modules.boss: Weekend review: a backfill meant to catch late trips double-counted a week of Finance revenue. Marcus and Kofi must show the merge on the trip key, the lookback window and why a rerun should change nothing it should not.
modules.finale: At the board meeting, completed and settled trips appear side by side, defined once in dbt, and both teams' numbers match. Kofi presents with Marcus. Lena's 2% gap stays in her notebook. Tom smiles: "Now make it real time."
modules.zoe: Zoe asks why grown-ups argued about counting. Marcus says, "We used one word for two different things, so we gave each its own name, and now everyone agrees."
